blocks.text: In positive feedback, the product or response made by the controlling system speeds up action of controlling system. An example of positive feedback is release of oxytocin hormone by posterior pituitary. During childbirth when uterus begins to contract, the sensory neurons send signals to hypothalamus. Hypothalamus triggers the release of oxytocin from posterior pituitary. Oxytocin stimulates uterus to produce more and stronger contractions. When hypothalamus receives message of stronger contractions, it triggers the release of more oxytocin. This series of positive feedback continues until the birth of baby.

blocks.alt: A cycle of five numbered boxes joined by arrows: 1 Uterus contracts and sensory neurons send signals to hypothalamus; 2 Hypothalamus triggers the release of oxytocin from posterior pituitary; 3 Oxytocin reaches uterus and stimulates it to produce more contractions; 4 Message of stronger contractions reaches hypothalamus; 5 Hypothalamus triggers the release of more oxytocin from posterior pituitary, which leads back to 1.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.7: Positive feedback of oxytocin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.7).

blocks.text: In negative feedback, the end product stops the initial step of the process. Negative feedback is common in endocrine system. For example, when blood glucose goes above normal, the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans sense release insulin. Insulin lowers blood glucose by doing different actions. Due to these actions, blood glucose level falls to normal. This result i.e., normal blood glucose level stimulates the beta cells to stop releasing insulin. Similarly, the release of glucagon is also controlled by negative feedback. When blood glucose level goes low, the alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete glucagon. This hormone takes actions to raise blood glucose. Due to these actions, blood glucose level rises to normal. This result i.e., normal blood glucose level stimulates the alpha cells to stop releasing glucagon.

blocks.alt: Two loops around a central box, Homeostasis: glucose level 90 mg/100mL. Upper (eating icecream): glucose rises above normal, beta cells release insulin, the liver takes up glucose, glucose falls to normal; a dashed arrow, negative feedback to stop insulin release, returns to the beta cells. Lower (skipping dinner): blood glucose falls below normal, alpha cells release glucagon, the liver breaks glycogen into glucose, blood glucose rises to normal; a dashed arrow stops glucagon release.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.8: Negative feedback of insulin and glucagon (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.8).
